bib.title: MERLOT RESERVE: Neural Script Knowledge through Vision and Language and Sound

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "MERLOT Reserve: Neural Script Knowledge through Vision and Language and Sound", Rowan Zellers, Jiasen Lu, Ximing Lu, Youngjae Yu, Yanpeng Zhao, Mohammadreza Salehi, Aditya Kusupati, Jack Hessel, Ali Farhadi, Yejin Choi (UW / AI2 / Edinburgh). The extraction prints only "arXiv:2201.02639v4 [cs.CV] 13 May 2022". No venue appears in the text, so cite it as arXiv 2022. (It is widely known as CVPR 2022, but the PDF does not say so.)

COVERAGE: I read all 151,037 chars over 30 pages: main text, Tables 1-11, Appendices A-F, and Figure 10. I skimmed the references for origins. pypdf output was garbled (a shifted font map, e.g. "RP million" for "20 million"), so I used the PyMuPDF extraction for everything, which is clean. Paths: /tmp/m2.txt (clean) and the source /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/08-multimodal-engineering/sources/zellers-2022-merlot-reserve.pdf

MOST USEFUL NUMBER ON AUDIO VS TRANSCRIPT: TVQA (Table 3). It uses one finetuned model, tested with subtitles only, audio only, or both (the two softmaxes averaged). For Reserve-L on test: subtitles 85.6, audio 84.8, both 86.1. On val: 85.9 / 85.6 / 86.5. For Reserve-B on val: 82.5 / 81.3 / 83.1. Audio alone scores slightly below the transcript (0.3 to 1.2 points). Adding it on top of the transcript gains about 0.5 to 0.6 points. So the transcript does most of the work, and audio adds a small gain on dialogue-heavy TV QA.

CLAIMS
- claim: Reserve learns joint video, audio and text representations. Snippets of text and audio are replaced with a MASK, and the model has to choose the correct masked-out snippet contrastively.
  number: 20 million videos
  setup: pretraining on YouTube
  quote: "Given a video, we replace snippets of text and audio with a MASK token; the model learns by choosing the correct masked-out snippet. Our objective learns faster than alternatives, and performs well at scale: we pretrain on 20 million YouTube videos."
  where: p1 abstract
- claim: Finetuned Reserve set the state of the art on VCR, TVQA and Kinetics-600.
  number: 5%, 7%, 1.5%
  setup: finetuned Reserve-L against prior work
  quote: "it sets state-of-the-art on Visual Commonsense Reasoning (VCR), TVQA, and Kinetics-600; outperforming prior work by 5%, 7%, and 1.5% respectively."
  where: p1 abstract
- claim: On TVQA, audio alone does about as well as subtitles, and combining the two is best.
  number: L test 85.6 (subtitles) / 84.8 (audio) / 86.1 (both). Prior SOTA MERLOT 78.4. Human 89.4.
  setup: Table 3. A single model is finetuned jointly on subtitle and audio copies of each sequence. "Both" averages the two softmax predictions. Each question uses 35 s of video around the annotated region.
  quote: "During training, each sequence is duplicated: we provide one sequence with subtitles from the video, and for the other, we use audio. This lets us train a single model, and then test how it will do given subtitles, given audio, or given both (by averaging the two softmax predictions)." and "Reserve-L improves over prior work by 7.6%."
  where: p6, Table 3
- claim: Adding audio during pretraining helps VCR, even though VCR has no sound.
  number: +0.7 (audio as target), +1.0 (audio as input and target), plus about 1 more point from web text
  setup: Table 1, VCR Q→A val after one pretraining epoch, same architecture and data throughout. Mask LM 67.2, VirTex-style 67.8, Contrastive Span 69.7, audio as target 70.4, audio as input and target 70.7, without strict localization 70.6, full Reserve-B 71.9.
  quote: "This boosts VCR accuracy by 0.7%." / "This boosts accuracy by 1% in total." / "Table 1: Ablation study of our contrastive span objective. It outperforms prior work in a Vision+Text setting, with a 1% boost when audio is added. Our full setup, adding written text, improves another 1%."
  where: p5
- claim: The contrastive span objective beats token-level Mask LM and VirTex on vision plus text alone.
  number: over 2%
  setup: Table 1, one epoch
  quote: "our contrastive span objective boosts performance by over 2%, after one epoch of pretraining only on vision and text."
  where: p5
- claim: On VCR test, Reserve-L beats every single model on the leaderboard.
  number: Q→AR 72.0 (vs MERLOT 65.1, ERNIE-ViL-Large 66.3)
  setup: Table 2, VCR test, single models
  quote: "Reserve-L outperforms all prior work, by over 5% on Q→AR metric."
  where: p6
- claim: On Kinetics-600, audio adds 1.7 points top-1.
  number: B 88.1→89.7. L 89.4→91.1 (MTV-Huge 89.6).
  setup: Table 4, val, finetuned jointly with and without audio. 4 uniformly sampled frames plus 6 audio subsegments (10 s).
  quote: "Reserve improves by 1.7% when it can jointly represent the video's frames with its sound."
  where: p6-7, Table 4, App D.1.3
- claim: Zero-shot, Reserve is competitive on four video tasks and beats supervised work on STAR. Audio helps on every task (here audio is added on top of frames, not compared against a transcript).
  number: STAR overall B 39.4→40.5 with audio (ClipBERT supervised 36.7). MSR-VTT QA top-1 L 5.8 with audio vs Just Ask 2.9. LSMDC L 31.0 with audio (CLIP ≤2.3). EPIC verb R@5 L 15.6→23.2 with audio.
  setup: Table 5, N=8 segments, labels encoded as phrases and nearest to MASK. Questions are rewritten as statements (templates for STAR, GPT-3 for MSR-VTT).
  quote: "Our base model outperforms all supervised prior work by 3.7%. The model with audio performs better, with average 1.1% improvement." and "Reserve-L (+audio) outperforms Reserve-L with an average 3.0%"
  where: p7, App D.2.1-D.2.2
- claim: On LSMDC, Reserve beats human text-only performance but not a supervised LSTM.
  number: 31% vs 30.2% (human), 34.4% (LSTM)
  setup: zero-shot fill-in-the-blank test, 30,354 examples
  quote: "Our model obtains 31% when audio is included, which outperforms human text-only performance (30.2 %) [82]... A supervised LSTM obtains 34.4% in this text-only setting"
  where: App D.2.3
- claim: Model sizes and compute.
  number: B about 200M finetunable parameters, L 644M. TPU v3-512 for 5 days (B) and 16 days (L).
  setup: B has hidden size 768, ViT-B/16 and a 12-layer joint encoder. L has 1024, ViT-L/16 and a 24-layer joint encoder. Both use a 12-layer audio encoder (AST-style) and a 4-layer text span encoder. Batch is 1024 videos × 16 segments, 10 epochs, 750k steps.
  quote: "We train on TPU v3-512 accelerators; training takes 5 days for Reserve-B, and 16 days for Reserve-L." / "Reserve-B has 200M finetunable parameters ... Reserve-L has 644M parameters."
  where: p4, p6, Table 8
- claim: Efficiency per VCR candidate.
  number: GFLOPs: B 146, L 341, MERLOT 303, UNITER-Large 1867
  setup: Table 7, one image plus 128 tokens
  quote: "our Reserve-L requires one-fifth the FLOPs of detector-based systems, like UNITER-Large"
  where: p6, Table 7
- claim: Dataset. YT-Temporal-1B contains 20M English-subtitled YouTube videos and 1B frames.
  number: 20M videos / 1B frames
  setup: crawled through YouTube recommendations from YT-Temporal-180M, filtered by a T5 groundedness classifier. Only video IDs are released.
  quote: "we introduce a new training dataset of 20 million English-subtitled YouTube videos, and 1 billion frames, called YT-Temporal-1B."
  where: p4, App E
- claim: Input design relevant to frame selection. A video is cut into 5 s segments, and each segment contributes one frame taken from its middle plus either its ASR text or its audio.
  number: 5 seconds
  setup: pretraining
  quote: "Segments default to 5 seconds in length" / "A frame vt, from the middle of the segment"
  where: p3
- claim: YouTube caption timestamps are slightly early and loose. The authors fit a regressor that corrects them by at most about 0.3 s.
  number: about 0.1 s early, correction ≤0.3 s
  setup: 2000 videos aligned against Google Cloud ASR
  quote: "they show up on average roughly 0.1 seconds before each word is spoken" / "the offsets can never be above 0.3 seconds"
  where: App C.1-C.2
- claim: Audio does not help person recognition. Reserve recognises celebrities far worse than CLIP.
  number: under 11% vs CLIP 86.0%
  setup: Table 6, 120 celebrities, zero-shot
  quote: "In all modes, our model is less than 11% accurate at recognizing celebrities."
  where: App A.1.1
- claim: Zero-shot audio classification lags supervised AudioCLIP.
  number: ESC50 52.2 vs 68.6. US8K 62.3 vs 68.8.
  setup: Table 11, image-and-text prompt
  quote: "AudioCLIP [54] ... performs 16% higher on ESC50, and 6.4% higher on US8K."
  where: App F.1
- claim: Energy use.
  number: 8.23 t CO2e, about 20,000 kWh
  setup: about 3 weeks on TPU v3-512, europe-west4
  quote: "The total carbon footprint of our work was a net 8.23 tons of CO2 equivalent"
  where: App A.4

LIMITS:
- The authors concede: "Our model only learns from 40-second long videos; relies on ASR models for subtitles, and can only match (not generate) text and audio."
- Zero-shot results depend on hand-written question-to-statement prompts. Reserve-L does worse than B on STAR, which the authors attribute to sensitivity to grammar.
- The audio-vs-transcript evidence comes from one task (TVQA, scripted TV) using averaged ensembles. No retrieval or RAG evaluation is reported.
- Pretraining may not have converged: "if we pretrained longer, VCR performance might continue to increase."
- NaN gradients in L were zeroed out ("We are not currently sure why this happens").
- The ASR was not cleaned, unlike MERLOT. Bias and privacy risks are acknowledged.
- Dated: this is a 2022 encoder-only matching model that does not generate. It predates LLM-based video models.

BUILDS ON: MERLOT (Zellers et al., 2021) for the frame-transcript matching objective and the data pipeline. CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) and ALIGN (Jia et al., 2021) for contrastive matching. BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) and SpanBERT (Joshi et al., 2020) for masking. VirTex (Desai & Johnson, 2021). ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020). AST (Gong et al., 2021). Rotary embeddings (Su et al., 2021). VATT (Akbari et al., 2021) for the Kinetics setup. The Pile (Gao et al., 2020) for web text. "Reentry" from Edelman (1993). Scripts from Schank & Abelson (1975).

CODE: none worth keeping. The paper has only the loss equation (Eq. 1: symmetric InfoNCE between L2-normalised MASK predictions and span encodings, scaled by a learned σ clipped at 100, p4) and the GPT-3 question-rewrite prompt (App D.2.4).

FIGURES:
- Fig 2 (p3) shows the architecture: ViT plus an audio encoder, with BPE text or audio at each segment, fused by a joint encoder. Faster than prose for "one frame plus text-or-audio per segment".
- Fig 3 (p4) shows contrastive span training with masked text and audio matched against independent encodings. It explains the objective at a glance.
- Fig 5 (p8) shows the popcorn and "why"-laugh examples where audio carries information the subtitles lack. It is the clearest intuition for when audio adds over a transcript.
- Fig 7 (p22) shows the misalignment between ASR timing and audio and the masking fix. Relevant to timestamped transcripts.

PROBLEMS:
- pypdf extraction is garbled (font mapping), so I used the PyMuPDF text instead.
- Internal inconsistency on FLOPs: the main text says Reserve-L "uses fewer FLOPs than MERLOT, while scoring 7% higher". Table 7 shows 341 GFLOPs for Reserve-L against 303 for MERLOT, and Appendix B.3 says "roughly on par", then "it [MERLOT] uses more FLOPs than does our Reserve-L". Don't cite the "fewer FLOPs" claim.
- Table 7 gives Reserve-L VCR Q→AR as 71.5, while Table 2 gives 72.0 on test. The split for Table 7 is not stated.
- Table 9 is described as finetuning hyperparameters, but D.1 calls it "Table 8".
- The paper contains no embedded instructions.
